body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Catch-up of adolescent vaccines through school-located clinics after pandemic disruption: coverage by grade and school","authors":"Haldane-Okoro M, Feng-Albright C, Duarte-Nkemelu S","year":2024,"venue":"Tarrowby Immunization Reports","doi":"10.5555/tir.2024.0203","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We describe a school-located catch-up program in 58 secondary schools after two disrupted school years. Using register data from before and six months after the program, coverage of the adolescent HPV series rose from 54 to 71 percent, meningococcal ACWY from 68 to 83 percent and the pertussis-containing booster from 70 to 84 percent. Gains were smallest in schools in the most deprived quintile, where HPV coverage rose from 41 to 52 percent. Schools that sent consent reminders by text message had higher consent return. The analysis relied on a register whose completeness for adolescents was not assessed."},{"title":"Completeness of a regional immunization register for adolescent vaccines compared with school vaccination cards","authors":"Sorensen-Baptiste L, Oyelowo-Kerr A","year":2021,"venue":"Register Science and Surveillance","doi":"10.5555/rss.2021.0102","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared register entries with vaccination cards for 1,480 students in 30 schools. The register agreed with the card for 91 percent of doses given in school programs and 78 percent of doses given in community clinics or pharmacies. Agreement was lowest for students who had moved into the region in the previous two years (64 percent). Register-based coverage underestimated card-based coverage by 4 to 9 percentage points, depending on the vaccine. The authors recommend a correction for doses given outside school programs when registers are used to measure coverage."},{"title":"Paper forms and text message reminders for parental consent in school vaccination programs","authors":"Mbeki-Lorenzo T, Whitfield-Arora N, Castell-Ibe O","year":2022,"venue":"Tarrowby Immunization Reports","doi":"10.5555/tir.2022.0317","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In a program covering 44 schools, consent forms were sent home on paper, and from the second term parents also received text message reminders with a link to an electronic form. Consent return rose from 61 to 79 percent after reminders were added. The rise was smaller in schools where more than a third of families spoke a language other than the program language at home (from 52 to 63 percent), and electronic forms were used less by parents in those schools. Translated reminders were introduced late and could not be evaluated separately."},{"title":"Neighbourhood deprivation and completion of adolescent vaccines in school programs: a cross-sectional analysis","authors":"Rahman-Ostrowski J, Beaumont-Addo K","year":2019,"venue":"Journal of Population Immunization","doi":"10.5555/jpi.2019.0055","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using linked school program and area data for 21,600 students, we examined HPV series completion by quintile of neighbourhood deprivation. Completion was 74 percent in the least deprived quintile and 49 percent in the most deprived, a gradient that persisted after adjustment for school and grade. Consent refusal explained less of the gap than consent forms that were never returned. Students absent on vaccination days were concentrated in the most deprived quintile. The analysis could not separate deprivation from the language spoken at home."},{"title":"Cluster sampling for school vaccination coverage surveys: design effects from twelve surveys","authors":"Kiplagat-Moreno D, Halvorsen-Pike R","year":2017,"venue":"Survey Methods in Public Health","doi":"10.5555/smph.2017.0009","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We pooled data from twelve school-based vaccination coverage surveys that sampled schools and then students within schools. Design effects for coverage estimates ranged from 1.6 to 2.8, with a median of 2.1, and were largest where coverage differed most between schools. Checking vaccination cards changed estimates by up to 11 percentage points compared with parent report. Response was lower among students whose parents had to return a card or form. We provide design effects to plan sample sizes for future surveys."},{"title":"Saturday community clinics as an adjunct to school vaccination: who attends?","authors":"Brenton-Achieng F, Lowe-Zamora P","year":null,"venue":"District public health service report series","providerType":"report","abstract":"Four district health units offered Saturday vaccination clinics alongside school visits during a catch-up campaign. Of 1,930 students vaccinated at Saturday clinics, 62 percent had missed a school visit through absence and 21 percent had returned a consent form too late for the school visit. Students from the most deprived neighbourhoods were under-represented at Saturday clinics relative to their share of missed doses. The report does not state its year of publication, and attendance was counted from clinic lists rather than the register."}]}
